items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

In this photograph taken by Lewis Hine in 1908 for the National Child Labor Committee, young children estimated to be between 8 and 12 years old stand barefoot beside large industrial spinning machines inside a cotton mill. The children are small compared to the machinery surrounding them and appear to be operating the spinning equipment on the factory floor.

(Photograph by Lewis Hine, 1908. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, National Child Labor Committee Collection.)

Which working conditions shown in the photograph most clearly demonstrate the dangers faced by child laborers in early twentieth-century textile factories?

choices.text: Children working barefoot near large, unguarded industrial machinery
Children performing outdoor agricultural labor in extreme heat
Children being forced to work overnight shifts without rest
Children denied access to clean drinking water during shifts

items.explanation: The photograph shows children barefoot and in close proximity to large industrial machinery, directly illustrating physical danger: unguarded moving parts, hard floors, and the risk of injury from equipment far larger than the children themselves. Hine deliberately captured these details to document hazardous conditions. The other choices reflect real issues of the era but are not what is directly visible in this specific image.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

In this photograph taken by Lewis Hine in 1908 for the National Child Labor Committee, young children estimated to be between 8 and 12 years old stand barefoot beside large industrial spinning machines inside a cotton mill. The children are small compared to the machinery surrounding them and appear to be operating the spinning equipment on the factory floor.

(Photograph by Lewis Hine, 1908. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, National Child Labor Committee Collection.)

How does this photograph connect to the goals of the Progressive Era reform movement in the early twentieth century?

choices.text: It was intended to recruit child workers for safer factory jobs created by Progressive legislation
It documented conditions that abolitionists used to argue against industrial expansion
It provided visual evidence reformers used to build public support for child labor laws
It illustrated how temperance reforms had improved conditions for factory workers

items.explanation: Progressive Era reformers believed that using documented evidence — photographs, reports, and investigative journalism — could awaken public conscience and pressure lawmakers to act. Hine's images for the National Child Labor Committee directly supported campaigns that led to state and eventually federal child labor regulations. The photograph is therefore both a documentary record and a reform tool. Choice A misidentifies the reformers' target audience; Choice B confuses the era with antebellum abolitionism; Choice D conflates child labor reform with temperance.

items.stem:
Use the photograph to answer the question.

In this photograph taken by Lewis Hine in 1908 for the National Child Labor Committee, young children estimated to be between 8 and 12 years old stand barefoot beside large industrial spinning machines inside a cotton mill. The children are small compared to the machinery surrounding them and appear to be operating the spinning equipment on the factory floor.

(Photograph by Lewis Hine, 1908. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, National Child Labor Committee Collection.)

Why were documentary photographs by reformers like Lewis Hine particularly effective at generating public support for child labor reform, compared to written investigative reports covering the same conditions?

choices.text: Photographs were more widely distributed through newspapers than written articles, reaching a larger audience
Photographs created immediate emotional and visual evidence that made conditions difficult to deny or dismiss
Photographs were accepted as legal evidence in court, making them more useful for prosecution than written testimony
Photographs allowed reformers to hide the identities of victims, making factory owners less likely to retaliate

items.explanation: Photographs provided immediate, undeniable visual proof of conditions that written reports described in abstract terms. Seeing real children — small, barefoot, dwarfed by machinery — created an emotional connection that statistics and narratives could not fully replicate. This made it difficult for opponents to dismiss the claims as exaggerated. Choice A is incorrect because photographs were not yet widespread in daily newspapers in this period in a way that gave them less credibility than text. Choice C overstates legal evidentiary standards. Choice D is the reverse of the reality: photographs depersonalized the scale by personalizing individual faces.

items.stem: What is a "trust" in business terms?

choices.text: A combination of companies organized to dominate an entire industry
choices.textEs: Una combinación de compañías organizadas para dominar una industria entera

choices.text: A legal agreement between business partners to share mutual resources
choices.textEs: Un acuerdo legal entre socios comerciales para compartir recursos mutuos

choices.text: A small family-owned business that operates within a single local area
choices.textEs: Un pequeño negocio familiar que opera dentro de una sola área local

choices.text: A government agency responsible for overseeing interstate trade rules
choices.textEs: Una agencia gubernamental responsable de supervisar reglas de comercio interestatal

items.explanation: A trust was a combination of companies placed under one management so they could dominate an industry and reduce competition. Choice B is wrong if it describes a simple partnership, because trusts were much larger arrangements designed to control markets. Choice D is wrong because a regulatory agency oversees business, while a trust is a private business structure. Trusts became one of the main symbols of monopoly power in the late 1800s.
items.explanationEs: Un fideicomiso es un arreglo legal donde múltiples compañías dan el control de sus acciones a una junta de fideicomisarios, creando efectivamente un monopolio o casi monopolio. John D. Rockefeller fue pionero en esta estrategia con el Fideicomiso Standard Oil, que controló múltiples compañías petroleras. Los fideicomisos eliminaron la competencia, fijaron precios y dominaron industrias enteras, llevando a la protesta pública y la legislación antimonopolio.

items.stem:
Use the political cartoon to answer the question.

The cartoon from Puck magazine shows Theodore Roosevelt wielding a large club labeled 'Big Stick' against moneybag figures representing industrial trusts, depicting his Progressive Era antitrust policies.

What does the 'Big Stick' label on Roosevelt's club most directly symbolize?

choices.text: The U.S. military, which Roosevelt deployed against striking workers
The labor union movement that supported Roosevelt's antitrust agenda
Presidential and federal power used to confront and regulate corporate monopolies
Public outrage that pressured Congress to pass antitrust legislation

items.explanation: C is correct: The 'Big Stick' refers to Roosevelt's foreign and domestic policy philosophy — 'speak softly and carry a big stick' — representing the use of executive power and government authority to confront and control powerful interests, in this context the industrial trusts. A is incorrect: the military was not the primary tool Roosevelt used against domestic trusts; he used legal and regulatory action. B is incorrect: the Big Stick represents federal power, not support for labor unions specifically. D is incorrect: the cartoon depicts Roosevelt using the stick against corporations, not as a symbol of public opinion.

items.stem: What was the significance of the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890?
items.stemEs: ¿Cuál fue la importancia de la Ley Antimonopolio Sherman de 1890?

choices.text: It banned workers from organizing into collective bargaining units
choices.textEs: Prohibió a los trabajadores organizarse en unidades de negociación colectiva

choices.text: It mandated federal government ownership of major industries
choices.textEs: Ordenó la propiedad del gobierno federal de las principales industrias

choices.text: It provided legal protections for business consolidation practices
choices.textEs: Proporcionó protecciones legales para prácticas de consolidación empresarial

choices.text: It was the first federal law attempting to restrict monopolies
choices.textEs: Fue la primera ley federal que intentó restringir los monopolios

items.explanation: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 was significant because it was the first federal law aimed at limiting monopolies and combinations that restrained trade. Choice A is wrong because the act did not ban unions, even though courts sometimes misused it against labor early on. Choice B is wrong because it did not put industries under government ownership. The law marked the start of federal antitrust policy during the age of big business.
items.explanationEs: La Ley Antimonopolio Sherman fue la primera ley federal diseñada para prohibir prácticas comerciales monopolísticas y fideicomisos que restringían el comercio. Sin embargo, inicialmente fue débil y vagamente redactada, lo que dificultó su aplicación. Irónicamente, se usó más efectivamente contra los sindicatos laborales que contra las grandes empresas en sus primeros años. La ley se volvió más efectiva durante la Era Progresista, particularmente bajo el presidente Theodore Roosevelt.

items.stem: How does Carnegie's "Gospel of Wealth" differ from pure Social Darwinism?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo difiere el "Evangelio de la Riqueza" de Carnegie del Darwinismo Social puro?

choices.text: Because building economic independence was achievable even under Jim Crow
choices.textEs: Carnegie creía que el gobierno debería redistribuir toda la riqueza equitativamente

choices.text: The strike was crushed after Pinkerton agents and state militia were used
choices.textEs: Carnegie apoyaba la propiedad estatal de las principales industrias y negocios

choices.text: Carnegie argued the wealthy had a duty to benefit society through giving
choices.textEs: Carnegie argumentó que los ricos tenían el deber de beneficiar a la sociedad dando

choices.text: Vertical integration - controlling all stages from raw materials to sales
choices.textEs: Carnegie creía que la acumulación individual de riqueza debería prohibirse

items.explanation: Andrew Carnegie’s “Gospel of Wealth” argued that rich people had a moral duty to use their fortunes for the public good through libraries, schools, and charities. A choice saying poverty proved moral failure is wrong because Carnegie accepted inequality but still believed the wealthy should help society. The idea revealed how some industrialists tried to justify vast fortunes while also promoting philanthropy.
items.explanationEs: Mientras el Darwinismo Social justificaba la riqueza sin obligación moral, el Evangelio de la Riqueza de Carnegie argumentaba que los ricos eran "fideicomisarios" que tenían la responsabilidad de usar sus fortunas para bibliotecas, universidades y otras instituciones públicas. Carnegie escribió: "El hombre que muere rico muere deshonrado." Combinó la creencia en la competencia y acumulación con el deber filantrópico.

items.stem:
Use the political cartoon to answer the question.

The Puck magazine cartoon shows Theodore Roosevelt swinging a club labeled 'Big Stick' at moneybag figures representing industrial trusts during the Progressive Era.

Roosevelt's campaign against industrial trusts is best understood as a response to which of the following conditions?

choices.text: Small businesses calling on the federal government to protect them from foreign competitors
A wave of immigration that disrupted American labor markets and industry
European nations forming economic alliances that threatened American trade dominance
Massive industrial monopolies that had accumulated enough power to undermine competition and corrupt government

items.explanation: D is correct: During the Gilded Age, massive industrial monopolies like Standard Oil, U.S. Steel, and railroad trusts had accumulated so much market power that they could fix prices, eliminate competition, and corrupt government. Roosevelt's trust-busting responded specifically to this concentration of economic power, using the Sherman Antitrust Act to break up some combinations deemed harmful to competition. A is incorrect: the cartoon depicts Roosevelt confronting trusts, not protecting them. B is incorrect: immigration and labor reform were separate Progressive Era issues not depicted here. C is incorrect: foreign policy rivalry is not the focus of this cartoon or Roosevelt's domestic trust policy.

items.stem: How did technological innovations during the Gilded Age both improve and harm American society?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo mejoraron y dañaron las innovaciones tecnológicas durante la Edad Dorada a la sociedad estadounidense?
items.correctAnswer: Technological innovations had dual effects: Positive - railroads, telegraphs, electricity, and steel production increased efficiency, connected the nation, created jobs, and improved standards of living. Negative - same technologies enabled monopolies, displaced workers, created dangerous working conditions, destroyed Native American ways of life (railroads and buffalo), and concentrated wealth in few hands.
items.explanation: Railroads, telegraphs, electricity, and mass steel production connected markets, sped communication, and increased industrial output during the Gilded Age. A strong response should also explain the harms these same technologies could bring, such as dangerous factory work, the rise of monopolies, worker displacement, and the destruction of Native American ways of life as railroads spread westward. This tension is important because industrial progress created modern America while also deepening inequality and conflict.
items.explanationEs: Las respuestas fuertes deben: (1) Identificar al menos 2-3 beneficios de la tecnología, (2) Identificar al menos 2-3 daños, (3) Explicar la naturaleza contradictoria del progreso tecnológico, (4) Proporcionar ejemplos específicos. Las respuestas avanzadas reconocen que el impacto de la tecnología depende del contexto social, económico y político.

items.stem:
Use the political cartoon to answer the question.

The Puck magazine cartoon shows Theodore Roosevelt wielding his 'Big Stick' against industrial trusts, portraying him as a forceful reformer challenging the economic power of corporate monopolies.

Historians debate whether Roosevelt was a genuine opponent of big business or a moderate who actually preserved corporate capitalism. Which evidence from your knowledge of his presidency best supports the argument that Roosevelt's trust-busting was selective and limited?

choices.text: Roosevelt refused to pursue any antitrust cases, preferring instead to negotiate privately with corporate leaders
Roosevelt distinguished between 'good trusts' and 'bad trusts,' targeting only those he deemed harmful while leaving many large corporations intact
Roosevelt's antitrust campaign quickly lost public support because most Americans opposed government regulation of business
Congress blocked all of Roosevelt's antitrust legislation, and courts struck down the Sherman Antitrust Act during his presidency

items.explanation: B is correct: Roosevelt himself distinguished between 'good trusts' (large, efficient corporations that he believed served the public) and 'bad trusts' (those that abused their power). He pursued only 44 antitrust cases during his presidency and allowed many large corporations to continue operating, suggesting his trust-busting was strategic and selective, not a wholesale attack on big business. A is incorrect: the cartoon depicts Roosevelt actively challenging trusts, not ignoring them. C is incorrect: Roosevelt's progressive reforms were politically popular; claiming he lost public support is inaccurate. D is incorrect: Congress, not the courts, created the Sherman Antitrust Act; and the courts did limit some antitrust actions, but this does not explain Roosevelt's own limited approach.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives: Studies Among the Tenements of New York (1890), available through the Library of Congress digital collections:

"Suppose we look into one of these houses... We find two, perhaps three, families on a floor, each in a room or two, with a common hall and stairs. The rooms are dark, the air foul, the drainage defective — where there is any at all. The street below is unpaved, or badly paved, and garbage is heaped in the gutters. Overcrowding is the curse of the tenement. Eight, ten, twelve people in two small rooms; men, women, and children huddled together without distinction of age or sex, with the consequent destruction of all the decencies of life."
— Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of immigration patterns (US.09) and urbanization challenges (US.10), write a constructed response that:
1. States a clear CLAIM about the relationship between mass immigration and the urban crisis described by Riis, identifying who bore primary responsibility for tenement conditions.
2. Provides at least TWO pieces of specific EVIDENCE — one from the excerpt and one from your knowledge of immigration patterns, nativist responses, or urban reform efforts — to support your claim.
3. Provides REASONING that connects your evidence to your claim and evaluates whether reformers like Riis addressed root causes or only symptoms of the urban crisis.

Your response should be one to two well-developed paragraphs.
items.stemEs:
Lee el siguiente fragmento de Jacob Riis, Cómo vive la otra mitad: Estudios entre los conventillos de Nueva York (1890), disponible en las colecciones digitales de la Biblioteca del Congreso:

"Supongamos que miramos dentro de una de estas casas... Encontramos dos, quizás tres familias en un piso, cada una en una o dos habitaciones, con un pasillo y escaleras comunes. Las habitaciones son oscuras, el aire es viciado, el drenaje es deficiente — cuando existe. La calle de abajo no está pavimentada o está mal pavimentada, y la basura se amontona en las cunetas. El hacinamiento es la maldición del conventillo. Ocho, diez, doce personas en dos pequeñas habitaciones; hombres, mujeres y niños amontonados sin distinción de edad o sexo, con la consiguiente destrucción de toda la decencia de la vida."
— Jacob Riis, Cómo vive la otra mitad, 1890

Usando este fragmento y tu conocimiento sobre los patrones de inmigración (US.09) y los desafíos de la urbanización (US.10), escribe una respuesta construida que:
1. Establezca un ARGUMENTO claro sobre la relación entre la inmigración masiva y la crisis urbana descrita por Riis, identificando quién tenía la responsabilidad principal de las condiciones en los conventillos.
2. Proporcione al menos DOS piezas de EVIDENCIA específica — una del fragmento y una de tu conocimiento sobre los patrones de inmigración, las respuestas nativistas o los esfuerzos de reforma urbana — para apoyar tu argumento.
3. Proporcione RAZONAMIENTO que conecte tu evidencia con tu argumento y evalúe si los reformadores como Riis abordaron las causas raíz o solo los síntomas de la crisis urbana.

Tu respuesta debe ser de uno a dos párrafos bien desarrollados.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response claims that while mass immigration contributed to overcrowding, primary responsibility lay with landlords, city governments, and industrial employers who exploited immigrants' vulnerability. The student uses Riis's description of "eight, ten, twelve people" in two rooms as evidence of structural failure in housing regulation, then supplements with knowledge: the wave of New Immigration (1880-1920) from Southern and Eastern Europe; tenement landlords collecting maximum rent for minimal maintenance; the failure of city governments to enforce sanitation codes; and the Tenement House Act of 1901 as a partial reform. Strong reasoning evaluates Riis: his photojournalism raised public awareness and influenced reform legislation, but his work also reflected nativist biases that blamed immigrants themselves, and did not address the low wages that forced families into overcrowded conditions.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.09, US.10 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):

4 — Exemplary: States a historically defensible claim that identifies specific agents of responsibility (landlords, city governments, employers, or immigrants themselves) and takes a clear position. Two or more pieces of evidence are provided: at least one from the excerpt (e.g., describing physical conditions) and at least one from outside knowledge (e.g., New Immigration waves, specific legislation, nativist responses such as the Chinese Exclusion Act or the Immigration Restriction League). Reasoning explicitly evaluates whether reform efforts addressed root causes and connects to long-term consequences. Synthesis spans US.09 and US.10 and may reference US.14 (muckrakers) or US.15 (Progressive reform).

3 — Proficient: Clear claim with two pieces of evidence. Reasoning present but evaluation of reform effectiveness is incomplete or undeveloped.

2 — Developing: Vague claim. One substantial piece of evidence. Reasoning is stated but not developed into an evaluation.

1 — Beginning: Minimal claim or summarizes the excerpt without analysis. Little outside knowledge applied.

0 — No response or off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: New Immigration (1880-1920) from Southern/Eastern Europe; "push and pull" factors (poverty, persecution vs. economic opportunity); the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) as a nativist policy response; the Tenement House Act of 1901 (NYC); settlement houses like Hull House (Jane Addams); boss machine politics and their exploitation of immigrant communities; the Immigration Restriction League; overcrowded neighborhoods such as New York's Lower East Side.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):

4 — Ejemplar: Establece un argumento históricamente defendible que identifica agentes específicos de responsabilidad y toma una posición clara. Dos o más piezas de evidencia: al menos una del fragmento y al menos una del conocimiento externo (p. ej., olas de Nueva Inmigración, legislación específica, respuestas nativistas). El razonamiento evalúa explícitamente si los esfuerzos de reforma abordaron las causas raíz. La síntesis abarca US.09 y US.10.

3 — Competente: Argumento claro con dos piezas de evidencia. El razonamiento está presente, pero la evaluación de la efectividad de la reforma está incompleta.

2 — En desarrollo: Argumento vago. Una pieza sustancial de evidencia. El razonamiento se menciona pero no se desarrolla en una evaluación.

1 — Inicial: Argumento mínimo o solo resume el fragmento sin análisis.

0 — Sin respuesta o fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: La Nueva Inmigración (1880-1920) de Europa del Sur y del Este; factores de expulsión y atracción; la Ley de Exclusión China (1882) como respuesta nativista; la Ley de Conventillos de 1901 (NYC); casas de acogida como Hull House (Jane Addams); el sistema de jefes políticos y su explotación de las comunidades de inmigrantes; la Liga de Restricción de la Inmigración; barrios superpoblados como el Lower East Side de Nueva York.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), available in the public domain through the Library of Congress and Project Gutenberg:

"Mr. Washington distinctly asks that Black people give up, at least for the present, three things — First, political power; Second, insistence on civil rights; Third, higher education of Negro youth — and concentrate all their energies on industrial education, and accumulation of wealth, and the conciliation of the South. This policy has been courageously and insistently advocated for over fifteen years, and has been triumphant for perhaps ten years. As a result of this tender of the palm-branch, what has been the return? In these years there have occurred: 1. The disfranchisement of the Negro. 2. The legal creation of a distinct status of civil inferiority for the Negro. 3. The steady withdrawal of aid from institutions for the higher training of the Negro."
— W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk, 1903

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of African American leadership strategies (US.17) and nativism and discrimination (US.09), write a constructed response that:
1. States a CLAIM about whether Washington's strategy of accommodation or Du Bois's strategy of protest was better suited to improve the conditions of African Americans during the Progressive Era, using specific historical evidence to defend your position.
2. Provides at least TWO pieces of specific EVIDENCE — one from the excerpt and one from your knowledge of Washington's Tuskegee program, Du Bois's NAACP, or the broader racial climate of the era — to support your claim.
3. Provides REASONING that connects the Washington-Du Bois debate to the broader question of how marginalized groups can most effectively advocate for equality within a hostile political system.

Your response should be one to two well-developed paragraphs.
items.stemEs:
Lee el siguiente fragmento de W.E.B. Du Bois, Las Almas del Pueblo Negro (1903), disponible en el dominio público a través de la Biblioteca del Congreso y Project Gutenberg:

"El señor Washington pide claramente que los negros abandonen, al menos por el momento, tres cosas: primero, el poder político; segundo, la insistencia en los derechos civiles; tercero, la educación superior de la juventud negra — y concentren todas sus energías en la educación industrial, la acumulación de riqueza y la conciliación con el Sur. Esta política ha sido defendida con valentía e insistencia durante más de quince años, y ha triunfado durante quizás diez años. Como resultado de esta oferta de la rama de olivo, ¿cuál ha sido la respuesta? En estos años han ocurrido: 1. La privación del derecho al voto del Negro. 2. La creación legal de un estatus distinto de inferioridad civil para el Negro. 3. La retirada constante de ayuda de las instituciones para la formación superior del Negro."
— W.E.B. Du Bois, Las Almas del Pueblo Negro, 1903

Usando este fragmento y tu conocimiento de las estrategias de liderazgo afroamericano (US.17) y el nativismo y la discriminación (US.09), escribe una respuesta construida que:
1. Establezca un ARGUMENTO sobre si la estrategia de acomodación de Washington o la estrategia de protesta de Du Bois era más adecuada para mejorar las condiciones de los afroamericanos durante la Era Progresista.
2. Proporcione al menos DOS piezas de EVIDENCIA específica — una del fragmento y una de tu conocimiento sobre el programa Tuskegee de Washington, la NAACP de Du Bois o el clima racial más amplio de la época.
3. Proporcione RAZONAMIENTO que conecte el debate Washington-Du Bois con la pregunta más amplia de cómo los grupos marginados pueden abogar más efectivamente por la igualdad.

Tu respuesta debe ser de uno a dos párrafos bien desarrollados.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response states a defensible claim — either position is acceptable if well-argued. A student arguing for Du Bois uses the excerpt's enumeration of three specific failures (disfranchisement, legal inferiority, withdrawal of educational funding) that occurred during Washington's "triumphant" period as evidence that accommodation produced no tangible gains. Outside knowledge evidence: the founding of the NAACP (1909) as a direct response to Washington's approach, Du Bois's Crisis magazine, and the legal challenges to Jim Crow laws. A student arguing for Washington might use Tuskegee's tangible record of graduates entering skilled trades, Washington's ability to secure Gilded Age patronage from industrialists like Carnegie, and the danger of direct protest in an era of widespread lynching. Strong reasoning synthesizes: both strategies were constrained by the same hostile environment, and the debate itself reveals the impossible position of Black Americans trying to achieve equality within a system that had formally committed itself to white supremacy.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.17, US.09 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):

4 — Exemplary: Takes a clear, defensible position on the Washington vs. Du Bois debate. Uses excerpt evidence (specifically Du Bois's enumerated failures of accommodation) and at least one specific outside knowledge evidence piece (Tuskegee Institute, Atlanta Compromise speech 1895, founding of NAACP 1909, Crisis magazine, Jim Crow laws, lynching statistics). Reasoning connects to the broader question of advocacy strategy for marginalized groups and acknowledges the constraints both leaders faced. Synthesis spans US.17 and US.09 and may connect to US.07 (Reconstruction's collapse) or US.15 (Progressive reform's racial limits).

3 — Proficient: Clear position with two evidence pieces. Reasoning present but does not develop the broader argument about advocacy strategy.

2 — Developing: Summarizes both strategies without taking a defended position. One evidence piece. Reasoning describes rather than evaluates.

1 — Beginning: Restates the debate without analysis. Minimal outside knowledge.

0 — No response or off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise speech (1895); Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute; Washington's financial patronage from Carnegie and Rockefeller; Du Bois's concept of the "Talented Tenth"; founding of the NAACP (1909) by Du Bois, Ida B. Wells, Mary Church Terrell, and others; Library of Congress, NAACP Records (loc.gov) magazine (founded 1910); Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) and the legal structure of Jim Crow; documented lynching statistics from the era (Wells's Southern Horrors, 1892); Washington's "Atlanta Compromise" and its political trade-offs for Black political rights.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):

4 — Ejemplar: Toma una posición clara y defendible en el debate Washington vs. Du Bois. Usa evidencia del fragmento (específicamente las fallas enumeradas por Du Bois) y al menos una pieza de conocimiento externo (Instituto Tuskegee, discurso del Compromiso de Atlanta de 1895, fundación de la NAACP en 1909, revista Crisis, leyes de Jim Crow, estadísticas de linchamientos). El razonamiento conecta con la pregunta más amplia sobre la estrategia de defensa para grupos marginados.

3 — Competente: Posición clara con dos piezas de evidencia. El razonamiento está presente pero no desarrolla el argumento más amplio.

2 — En desarrollo: Resume ambas estrategias sin tomar una posición defendida. Una pieza de evidencia. El razonamiento describe en lugar de evaluar.

1 — Inicial: Reafirma el debate sin análisis. Conocimiento externo mínimo.

0 — Sin respuesta o fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Discurso del Compromiso de Atlanta de Booker T. Washington (1895); Instituto Normal e Industrial Tuskegee; financiación de Washington por Carnegie y Rockefeller; concepto de la "Décima Talentosa" de Du Bois; fundación de la NAACP (1909); revista Crisis (fundada en 1910); Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) y la estructura legal de Jim Crow; estadísticas de linchamientos documentadas (Horrores del Sur de Wells, 1892).

items.stem:
DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze each of the following three documents using the SOAPS framework (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Significance). Then construct a well-organized argument that responds to the prompt.

PROMPT: How effectively did Progressive Era reformers respond to the challenges created by mass immigration and urbanization between 1890 and 1920? In your argument, evaluate whether Progressive reforms addressed the structural conditions that made urban poverty possible, or whether they primarily managed its most visible symptoms while leaving the underlying causes intact. Use evidence from all three documents and at least two outside historical facts.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 1
Source: Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives: Studies Among the Tenements of New York, Chapter I, 1890. Library of Congress digital collections.

"Long ago it was said that 'one half of the world does not know how the other half lives.' That was true then. It did not know because it did not care. The half that was on top cared little for the struggles, and less for the fate of those who were underneath, so long as it was able to hold them there and keep its own seat... The Problem of the Poor in New York is their own ignorance: ignorance of the possibilities of life in this land of freedom; ignorance of the right to demand better conditions; ignorance, in short, of the very existence of a problem."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 2
Source: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House, Chapter V, 1910. Library of Congress digital collections.

"Hull-House was soberly opened on the theory that the dependence of classes on each other is reciprocal; and that as the social relation is essentially a reciprocal relation, it gives a form of expression that has value for both sides. The residents of Hull-House were not going to that neighborhood to help people, but to try to understand them, and perchance to learn from them what could not be learned from books. The neighbors were quite as important an element of the settlement as its residents, and their lives were fully as significant as those of the educated visitors."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 3
Source: Seventeenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified April 8, 1913. National Archives, Washington, D.C.

"The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, elected by the people thereof, for six years; and each Senator shall have one vote. The electors in each State shall have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures. When vacancies happen in the representation of any State in the Senate, the executive authority of such State shall issue writs of election to fill such vacancies."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Remember to apply SOAPS to each document, construct a clear argument, use all three documents as evidence, and add at least two outside historical facts to your response.
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: Analiza cada uno de los tres documentos siguientes usando el marco SOAPS (Orador, Ocasión, Audiencia, Propósito, Significado). Luego construye un argumento bien organizado que responda al enunciado.

ENUNCIADO: ¿Con qué efectividad respondieron los reformadores de la Era Progresista a los desafíos creados por la inmigración masiva y la urbanización entre 1890 y 1920? En tu argumento, evalúa si las reformas progresistas abordaron las condiciones estructurales que hacían posible la pobreza urbana, o si principalmente manejaron sus síntomas más visibles dejando intactas las causas subyacentes. Usa evidencia de los tres documentos y al menos dos hechos históricos externos.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 1
Fuente: Jacob Riis, Cómo vive la otra mitad: Estudios entre los conventillos de Nueva York, Capítulo I, 1890. Colecciones digitales de la Biblioteca del Congreso.

"Hace mucho tiempo se dijo que 'una mitad del mundo no sabe cómo vive la otra mitad.' Eso era verdad entonces. No lo sabía porque no le importaba. La mitad que estaba arriba se preocupaba poco por las luchas, y menos por el destino de quienes estaban debajo, siempre que pudiera mantenerlos allí y conservar su propio lugar... El problema de los pobres en Nueva York es su propia ignorancia: ignorancia de las posibilidades de vida en esta tierra de libertad."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 2
Fuente: Jane Addams, Veinte Años en Hull-House, Capítulo V, 1910. Colecciones digitales de la Biblioteca del Congreso.

"Hull-House se abrió sobriamente con la teoría de que la dependencia de las clases entre sí es recíproca; y que como la relación social es esencialmente una relación recíproca, da una forma de expresión que tiene valor para ambos lados. Los residentes de Hull-House no iban a ese vecindario para ayudar a la gente, sino para tratar de entenderla, y quizás para aprender de ella lo que no se podía aprender de los libros."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 3
Fuente: Decimoséptima Enmienda a la Constitución de los Estados Unidos, ratificada el 8 de abril de 1913. Archivos Nacionales, Washington, D.C.

"El Senado de los Estados Unidos se compondrá de dos Senadores de cada Estado, elegidos por el pueblo del mismo, por seis años; y cada Senador tendrá un voto. Los electores de cada Estado tendrán los requisitos necesarios para los electores de la rama más numerosa de las legislaturas estatales."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Recuerda aplicar SOAPS a cada documento, construir un argumento claro, usar los tres documentos como evidencia y agregar al menos dos hechos históricos externos.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response constructs a qualified argument: Progressive reformers made meaningful gains in addressing the symptoms of urban poverty through journalism, settlement houses, and democratic reform, but fundamentally failed to challenge the economic structures — low wages, long hours, unregulated landlords — that produced urban poverty in the first place. SOAPS for Document 1 — Riis: Speaker: Danish-American photojournalist and reformer; Occasion: Progressive-era reform movement gaining momentum; Audience: middle-class New Yorkers with political influence; Purpose: to shock the comfortable into demanding reform through graphic documentary; Significance: Riis frames the problem partly as immigrant ignorance, revealing nativist assumptions embedded in the reform movement. Document 2 — Addams: Speaker: co-founder of Hull-House and Nobel Peace Prize laureate; Occasion: Progressive peak period; Audience: middle-class readers and reform advocates; Purpose: to explain the settlement house philosophy as mutual learning rather than charity; Significance: Addams's reciprocity framework was more sophisticated than Riis's but still operated within the existing economic system. Document 3 — 17th Amendment: Speaker: U.S. Congress; Occasion: Progressive democratic reform; Audience: American voters; Purpose: to remove Senate corruption by allowing direct election; Significance: addresses political corruption but not economic inequality. Outside knowledge: the Immigration Act of 1917 (literacy tests) and 1924 Immigration Restriction Act show that Progressive "reform" ultimately included nativist restriction; the Tenement House Act (1901) improved some conditions but enforcement was inconsistent; wages for unskilled immigrant workers remained below subsistence without minimum wage legislation.

6 — Exemplary: Constructs a clear, historically defensible argument responsive to the structural vs. symptomatic reform distinction in the prompt. Applies SOAPS to all three documents, with at least one SOAPS element per document used as direct argument evidence. Incorporates two or more outside historical facts. Demonstrates cross-document synthesis (e.g., comparing Riis's and Addams's reform philosophies, or connecting the 17th Amendment to political but not economic democracy). Addresses both structural conditions and their management. Response is organized with thesis, body paragraphs, and conclusion.

5 — Advanced: Strong argument with SOAPS applied to all three documents. Two outside facts. Cross-document synthesis present. Minor gaps in analysis or organization.

4 — Proficient: Clear argument with SOAPS applied to at least two documents. One outside fact. Structural vs. symptomatic distinction addressed but incompletely.

3 — Adequate: Argument present but may focus on description over evaluation. SOAPS applied to one document. One outside fact or general knowledge applied.

2 — Developing: Summarizes the documents without constructing an argument about effectiveness. No SOAPS or minimal application. No specific outside knowledge.

1 — Beginning: Lists document information without argument or analysis.

0 — No response or off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS (SOAPS):
Doc 1 — Riis: Speaker's Danish immigrant background and photojournalism methods; nativist assumptions embedded in framing immigrant poverty as "ignorance"; the shock-journalism purpose and its effective mobilization of middle-class reform politics.
Doc 2 — Addams: The reciprocity framework as a critique of top-down charity; the middle-class position of settlement house workers and its limits; Hull-House as a model for both service provision and social research.
Doc 3 — 17th Amendment: The structural political reform targeting Senate corruption and machine politics; what direct election of senators addressed (political accountability) and did not address (economic power, wage levels, housing).

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: New York Tenement House Act (1901); Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) and Immigration Restriction League as nativist responses; Immigration Act of 1917 (literacy tests); immigration restriction act of 1924; Triangle Shirtwaist fire (1911) and subsequent NY labor laws; the 16th Amendment (income tax, 1913) as a more structural reform; machine politics and Tammany Hall's role in immigrant communities; AFL exclusion of unskilled, immigrant, and Black workers; Boss Tweed and the corruption that motivated the 17th Amendment.

DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze each document using the HIPP framework. Then construct a well-organized argument that responds to the prompt.

PROMPT: The Progressive Era produced multiple strategies for addressing racial inequality in America. Using all three documents and at least two outside historical facts, evaluate how effectively these strategies challenged the systemic racial exclusion that characterized the Gilded Age and Progressive Era. In your argument, explain why different leaders proposed different approaches, and assess whether any of these strategies produced lasting structural change in the position of African Americans in American society by 1920.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 1
Source: Booker T. Washington, "Atlanta Compromise" speech delivered at the Cotton States and International Exposition, Atlanta, Georgia, September 18, 1895. Reprinted in Up From Slavery (1901); available through the Library of Congress and Project Gutenberg.

"To those of my race who depend on bettering their condition in a foreign land or who underestimate the importance of cultivating friendly relations with the Southern white man, who is their next-door neighbor, I would say: "Cast down your bucket where you are" — cast it down in making friends in every manly way of the people of all races by whom we are surrounded. Cast it down in agriculture, mechanics, in commerce, in domestic service, and in the professions... In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 2
Source: W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk, Chapter III ("Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others"), 1903. Library of Congress and Project Gutenberg.

"Mr. Washington represents in Negro thought the old attitude of adjustment and submission; but adjustment at such a peculiar time as to make his programme unique. This is an age of unusual economic development, and Mr. Washington's programme naturally takes an economic cast, becoming a gospel of Work and Money to such an extent as apparently almost completely to overshadow the higher aims of life. Moreover, this is an age when the more advanced races are coming in closer contact with the less developed races, and the friction of varied interests is becoming acute... Mr. Washington's programme practically accepts the alleged inferiority of the Negro races."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 3
Source: Ida B. Wells, Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases, Chapter II, 1892. Originally published by the New York Age; available through the Library of Congress.

"The South's position is: Lynch law is better than no law at all... The Afro-American is not a bestial race. If this work can contribute in any way toward proving this, and at the same time arouse the conscience of the American people to a demand for justice to every citizen, and ultimate punishment of outlaws, I shall feel I have done my race a service. Other lands have their martyrs, too... The appeal of Southern Horrors is to the white man's sense of justice. It is not a demand — it is an appeal. But the appeal is backed by facts. Facts that make it irresistible."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Apply HIPP to each document, construct a clear argument, use all three documents as evidence, and incorporate at least two outside historical facts.

PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: Analiza cada documento usando el marco HIPP. Luego construye un argumento bien organizado que responda al enunciado.

ENUNCIADO: La Era Progresista produjo múltiples estrategias para abordar la desigualdad racial en América. Usando los tres documentos y al menos dos hechos históricos externos, evalúa cuán efectivamente estas estrategias desafiaron la exclusión racial sistémica que caracterizó la Era Dorada y la Era Progresista. En tu argumento, explica por qué diferentes líderes propusieron diferentes enfoques, y evalúa si alguna de estas estrategias produjo cambios estructurales duraderos en la posición de los afroamericanos en la sociedad estadounidense para 1920.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 1
Fuente: Booker T. Washington, discurso del "Compromiso de Atlanta" pronunciado en la Exposición de los Estados del Algodón e Internacional, Atlanta, Georgia, 18 de septiembre de 1895. Reimpreso en Cómo salí de la esclavitud (1901); disponible en la Biblioteca del Congreso y Project Gutenberg.

"A los de mi raza que dependen de mejorar su condición en tierra extranjera o que subestiman la importancia de cultivar relaciones amistosas con el hombre blanco del Sur, que es su vecino de al lado, yo les diría: 'Echen el cubo donde están' — échenlo haciendo amigos de todas las maneras viriles de la gente de todas las razas que nos rodea... En todas las cosas que son puramente sociales podemos ser tan separados como los dedos, pero uno como la mano en todas las cosas esenciales para el progreso mutuo."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 2
Fuente: W.E.B. Du Bois, Las Almas del Pueblo Negro, Capítulo III ("Del Sr. Booker T. Washington y Otros"), 1903. Biblioteca del Congreso y Project Gutenberg.

"El Sr. Washington representa en el pensamiento negro la antigua actitud de ajuste y sumisión; pero ajuste en un momento tan peculiar que hace que su programa sea único... El programa del Sr. Washington prácticamente acepta la supuesta inferioridad de las razas negras."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 3
Fuente: Ida B. Wells, Horrores del Sur: La ley del linchamiento en todas sus fases, Capítulo II, 1892. Publicado originalmente por el New York Age; disponible en la Biblioteca del Congreso.

"La posición del Sur es: La ley del linchamiento es mejor que ninguna ley... El afroamericano no es una raza bestial... La apelación de Horrores del Sur es al sentido de justicia del hombre blanco. No es una demanda — es una apelación. Pero la apelación está respaldada por hechos. Hechos que la hacen irresistible."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Aplica HIPP a cada documento, construye un argumento claro, usa los tres documentos como evidencia e incorpora al menos dos hechos históricos externos.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response argues that while Washington, Du Bois, and Wells each represented a distinct and internally coherent strategy, none produced lasting structural change by 1920 — because all three were operating against a system of racial exclusion that was legally entrenched (Plessy v. Ferguson, 1896), economically reinforced (disenfranchisement, sharecropping), and protected by organized violence (lynching). HIPP Document 1 — Washington: Historical context: speaking at a moment of maximum vulnerability for Black Southerners — Reconstruction has ended, Plessy is one year away, and lynching is at its peak; Intended audience: both white Southerners whose approval Washington needed and Black Southerners he was counseling; Purpose: to secure the political survival of Black institutions within a white-supremacist system; POV: a man born into slavery who saw industrial education as a realistic survival strategy given the absence of federal protection — revealing the context-dependence of his "accommodationism." Document 2 — Du Bois: Historical context: seven years after the Atlanta Compromise, with disfranchisement, legal inferiority, and educational withdrawal documented; Audience: Black intellectuals and sympathetic whites; Purpose: to demolish the theoretical foundation of accommodation by showing its measurable failures; POV: a Harvard-trained academic who could analyze macro trends Washington's institution-building could not address — but whose protest strategy also had limited structural leverage without federal enforcement. Document 3 — Wells: Historical context: 1892 — peak of lynching era, the same year she was driven from Memphis; Audience: "the white man's sense of justice" — framing the appeal for political survival; Purpose: to document racial terror using factual evidence to make it impossible to deny; POV: a journalist using the tools of her trade to challenge a system — but one who also recognized the limits of moral appeal when violence was state-sanctioned. Outside knowledge: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) as constitutional sanction for racial exclusion; the founding of the NAACP (1909) as institutionalization of Du Bois's protest strategy; continued lynching statistics (3,000+ documented lynchings 1882-1930); the Great Migration beginning ca. 1910 as Black Americans' ultimate strategic response to Southern racial terror — voting with their feet.

SCORING GUIDE (6 points):

Incorporates two or more outside historical facts. Cross-document synthesis: e.g., connecting Washington's context (1895, no federal protection) to Du Bois's 1903 critique (accommodation has produced measurable losses), or connecting Wells's factual documentation strategy to both muckraking (US.14) and to Du Bois's later NAACP legal strategy. Evaluates lasting structural change by 1920 and explains why it remained limited.

5 — Advanced: Strong argument with HIPP of all three documents. Two outside facts. Cross-document synthesis present. Assessment of lasting structural change present but less fully developed.

4 — Proficient: Clear argument with HIPP of two documents. One outside fact. Differences in strategy explained and assessed, but the structural change question is addressed only partially.

3 — Adequate: Takes a position on one strategy's effectiveness. HIPP of one document. One outside fact.

2 — Developing: Summarizes the three strategies without argument. Limited HIPP.

1 — Beginning: Lists document information without analysis.

0 — No response or off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); the Atlanta Compromise (1895) and Tuskegee's practical industrial training record; Du Bois's "Talented Tenth" concept; founding of the NAACP (1909); Library of Congress, NAACP Records (loc.gov) magazine (1910); Wells's documentation of lynching statistics and her exile from Memphis; the Great Migration (ca. 1910-1930) as a structural response to Southern racial terror; Wilson's segregation of the federal civil service (1913); lynching continued despite NAACP campaigns for federal anti-lynching legislation (repeatedly blocked in Congress 1918-1922); the 15th Amendment's failure to protect Black voting rights in practice.

6 — Ejemplar: Construye un argumento sofisticado sobre la efectividad de múltiples estrategias de equidad racial y explica por qué se adoptó cada una dado su contexto histórico específico. 0 — Sin respuesta o fuera del tema.

Ferguson (1896); el Compromiso de Atlanta (1895) y el historial práctico de formación industrial de Tuskegee; concepto de la "Décima Talentosa" de Du Bois; fundación de la NAACP (1909); revista Crisis (1910); documentación de Wells sobre estadísticas de linchamiento y su exilio de Memphis; la Gran Migración (ca. 1910-1930); segregación del servicio civil federal por Wilson (1913); el linchamiento continuó a pesar de las campañas de la NAACP por legislación federal antilinchamiento; fracaso de la 15ª Enmienda en proteger los derechos de voto de los afroamericanos en la práctica.

items.stem:
Extended Response: No sources are provided. Draw on your knowledge of United States history to construct your argument.

PROMPT: Between 1880 and 1920, approximately 20 million immigrants arrived in the United States, most from Southern and Eastern Europe. They transformed American cities, labor markets, and political culture — and triggered powerful nativist responses that shaped both immigration restriction and Progressive reform.

Write an extended response in which you construct a historically defensible argument that evaluates the following claim:

"The Progressive Era's response to mass immigration was fundamentally contradictory: reformers simultaneously worked to improve the material conditions of immigrant communities and to restrict immigration itself, revealing that Progressive ideology was shaped as much by nativist anxiety as by democratic idealism."

In your response:
- State a clear CLAIM that agrees, disagrees, or qualifies the statement.
- Provide at least THREE specific pieces of EVIDENCE from your knowledge of immigration (US.09), urbanization (US.10), and Progressive reform (US.15) that support your claim.
- Provide REASONING that explicitly connects your evidence to your claim and addresses the specific tension between reform and restriction.
- Demonstrate SYNTHESIS by connecting the contradictions of Progressive immigration policy to either the earlier Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) or the later Immigration Act of 1924, showing that the Progressive Era's response was part of a longer pattern in American immigration policy.

Your response should be two to three well-developed paragraphs.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida: No se proporcionan fuentes. Basa tu respuesta en tu conocimiento de la historia de los Estados Unidos.

ENUNCIADO: Entre 1880 y 1920, aproximadamente 20 millones de inmigrantes llegaron a los Estados Unidos, la mayoría de Europa del Sur y del Este. Transformaron las ciudades, los mercados laborales y la cultura política de América — y desencadenaron poderosas respuestas nativistas que dieron forma tanto a la restricción de la inmigración como a la reforma progresista.

Escribe una respuesta extendida en la que construyas un argumento históricamente defendible que evalúe la siguiente afirmación:

"La respuesta de la Era Progresista a la inmigración masiva fue fundamentalmente contradictoria: los reformadores trabajaron simultáneamente para mejorar las condiciones materiales de las comunidades de inmigrantes y para restringir la inmigración misma, revelando que la ideología progresista estaba moldeada tanto por la ansiedad nativista como por el idealismo democrático."

En tu respuesta:
- Establece un ARGUMENTO claro que esté de acuerdo, en desacuerdo o matice la afirmación.
- Proporciona al menos TRES piezas específicas de EVIDENCIA de tu conocimiento sobre la inmigración (US.09), la urbanización (US.10) y la reforma progresista (US.15) que apoyen tu argumento.
- Proporciona RAZONAMIENTO que conecte explícitamente tu evidencia con tu argumento y aborde la tensión específica entre la reforma y la restricción.
- Demuestra SÍNTESIS conectando las contradicciones de la política de inmigración progresista ya sea con la anterior Ley de Exclusión China (1882) o con la posterior Ley de Inmigración de 1924, mostrando que la respuesta de la Era Progresista fue parte de un patrón más largo en la política de inmigración de los EE.UU.

Tu respuesta debe ser de dos a tres párrafos bien desarrollados.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response argues that the claim is substantially accurate: Progressive reformers were genuinely contradictory in their approach to immigration, helping immigrants in their neighborhoods while supporting restrictions at the border. Evidence (1): Settlement houses like Hull-House provided education, childcare, labor advocacy, and community services that materially improved immigrant conditions — genuine reform motivated by democratic idealism. Evidence (2): The Immigration Restriction League (founded 1894 by Boston Brahmin reformers) overlapped significantly with the Progressive movement in membership and philosophy — many who supported settlement houses also supported literacy tests for immigrants, revealing nativist assumptions embedded in Progressive thought. Evidence (3): The Immigration Act of 1917 (passed during the Progressive peak) established a literacy test requirement — a mechanism designed specifically to restrict Southern and Eastern European immigration — reflecting the racial hierarchy embedded in Progressive reform ideology. The reasoning connects: the contradiction is not accidental but structural — Progressive ideology sought to reform the poor immigrant who was already here while restricting the "wrong kind" of immigrant from arriving, revealing that Progressive "improvement" required immigrants to assimilate to Anglo-Protestant norms. Synthesis: connects to Chinese Exclusion Act (1882), which established the precedent that the U.S. could exclude specific racial/national groups, and to the Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed Act), which used "national origins" quotas based on 1890 census data to dramatically restrict Southern/Eastern Europeans while effectively banning Asian immigration — the logical conclusion of the nativist strain within Progressive-era thinking.

4 — Exemplary: States a clear, historically defensible claim that takes a nuanced position on the contradiction within Progressive immigration policy. Provides three or more specific evidence pieces spanning US.09, US.10, and US.15. Reasoning explicitly addresses the tension between reform and restriction and explains WHY reformers were contradictory (not just THAT they were). Synthesis connects to either Chinese Exclusion (1882) as a precedent or the Immigration Act of 1924 as a consequence, with explicit reasoning about the longer pattern. Response is 2-3 paragraphs, well-organized.

3 — Proficient: Clear claim. Two to three evidence pieces. Reasoning addresses reform vs. restriction tension but does not fully explain the ideological roots of the contradiction. Synthesis present but not fully integrated.

2 — Developing: Claim is present but may address only the reform OR restriction side without the contradiction. Two evidence pieces. Reasoning present but undeveloped. Synthesis absent or mentioned without development.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: New Immigration waves (1880-1920) — Italians, Jews, Poles, Greeks, Slavs; push factors (poverty, persecution, pogroms); pull factors (industrial jobs, family networks, advertising by steamship companies); settlement houses (Hull-House, Henry Street Settlement); tenement conditions (Riis, How the Other Half Lives); Immigration Restriction League (1894); Dillingham Commission (1911) — classified immigrants by race and recommended restriction; Immigration Act of 1917 (literacy test); the "Americanization" movement in public schools; initiative, referendum, recall as Progressive democratic tools (US.15) that simultaneously excluded immigrant voters through nativist state politics.

SYNTHESIS EXPECTATIONS: Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) — the first racially targeted federal immigration restriction, establishing legal precedent that Progressive-era reformers extended to other groups; OR Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed) — the fulfillment of the restriction agenda begun in the Progressive Era, using 1890 census data (before the New Immigration peak) to set quotas that almost entirely excluded Southern and Eastern Europeans and formally banned Asian immigration.

4 — Ejemplar: Establece un argumento claro y históricamente defendible que toma una posición matizada sobre la contradicción dentro de la política de inmigración progresista. Proporciona tres o más piezas específicas de evidencia que abarcan US.09, US.10 y US.15. EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Olas de Nueva Inmigración (1880-1920) — italianos, judíos, polacos, griegos, eslavos; factores de expulsión y atracción; casas de acogida (Hull-House, Henry Street Settlement); condiciones de los conventillos; Liga de Restricción de la Inmigración (1894); Comisión Dillingham (1911); Ley de Inmigración de 1917 (prueba de alfabetización); el movimiento de "americanización" en las escuelas públicas.

EXPECTATIVAS DE SÍNTESIS: Ley de Exclusión China (1882) — la primera restricción de inmigración federal racialmente dirigida, estableciendo un precedente legal que los reformadores de la era progresista extendieron a otros grupos; O Ley de Inmigración de 1924 (Johnson-Reed) — el cumplimiento de la agenda de restricción comenzada en la Era Progresista.
